paintings.why: A kitchen glows with blue walls, a table and sunlight pouring in. Ludvig Karsten was a Norwegian painter who liked strong colors and bold shapes. He lived a free artist's life and painted with a loose, vivid touch. It's a bright, modern look at an ordinary room.
l: National Museum of Art, Architecture and Design

paintings.why: A guitar, a glass and a few fruit are tucked into bright blocks of yellow, orange, blue and green in this 1913 painting by Juan Gris, who said that Cubism was like building a picture from pieces.

paintings.t: L'Homme au hamac (Man in a Hammock)
paintings.why: A man rests in a hammock, among shapes that look like pieces of a puzzle. Albert Gleizes, a French Cubist who wrote about Cubism, painted this in 1913.

A woman from the Isthmus of Tehuantepec in southern Mexico wears the beautiful, embroidered dress and headdress of her region. Saturnino Herrán celebrated Mexican folk culture in his paintings. The Tehuana dress later became famous because Frida Kahlo wore it. It's a colorful portrait of Mexican heritage.

Circles, bright discs and a tiny propeller whirl across the canvas in honor of Louis Blériot, the first person to fly an airplane across the English Channel. Robert Delaunay painted this tribute to flight in 1914.

Flags, medals, an iron cross and bits of letters and numbers make a portrait of a person with no face. Marsden Hartley painted it in Berlin in 1914 in memory of his close friend Karl von Freyburg, a German soldier who was killed in the first months of World War I.

A girl in a white dress with long red hair looks calmly out of the picture. Eilif Peterssen painted many portraits of leading Norwegians and their families. This one comes from late in his career. It's a gentle, graceful portrait.

A man's face and body are broken into overlapping shapes and letters, in a Cubist style Popova brought from Paris to Russia. She painted this in 1915 and died of scarlet fever in 1924 at the age of 35.

paintings.t: Two models, Epi and Gertie, in the Amsterdam Fashion House Hirsch
paintings.why: Two fashion models in elegant dresses at a fashion house in Amsterdam, painted with quick, confident strokes. Isaac Israëls was fascinated by modern fashion and city life. He painted this when he was in his fifties. It's a stylish picture of the Jazz Age.

Three men sit around a card table and a lamp in a picture that has been turned into flat colors and straight lines. Theo van Doesburg, the founder of the De Stijl magazine, painted this in 1916 on his way to pure abstraction.
Dark and light blocks fit together like a puzzle in the De Stijl movement's style. Theo van Doesburg made this in 1917 from a painting of card players that he turned into pure rectangles.

A circus clown, Harlequin, holds a guitar in a patchwork of blue, black and white diamonds. Juan Gris painted this in 1917, and Harlequin, a character from Italian comedy, was a favorite of the Cubists.

The German poet Goethe, in a dressing gown, reads a book in a room full of women in an imagined Ottoman harem. Abdülmecid II painted this in 1918, and he was the last caliph of the Ottoman family and also a talented painter. It shows how Ottoman artists were interested in European culture. It's a very unusual meeting of East and West.

A woman in a robe stands in a swirl of orange-red flames, her hair and clothing streaming behind her. Uemura Shōen, one of Japan's greatest women painters, painted this in 1918, based on a legend of jealousy from a Noh play. The flames seem to come from her own feelings. It's a powerful picture by a master artist.

A large white square, a blue patch and a yellow bar are divided by thin black lines in Mondrian's Tableau I from 1921. Mondrian was a Dutchman who lived in Paris and later in New York, where he loved jazz and dancing.

A man in a dark jacket with a long face sits against a swirly background, painted with thick brushstrokes. Soutine painted this portrait in the early 1920s, before he became famous. The strong colors and lively shapes show how he used paint to express feeling. It's a typical example of his unique style.
Pigs on a fair carousel spin round and round in circles of color, in a playful painting by Robert Delaunay of 1922. It's also a joke: the pigs look like they are heading for the ring.

A fluffy tabby cat looks out at us with bright green eyes, sitting calmly with its fur painted in very fine lines. Takeuchi Seihō was a master painter from Kyoto who loved animals. The picture became a cultural treasure of Japan. It is one of the most famous cat paintings in the world.
paintings.k: Look at the cat's fur. The artist painted each tiny hair! What is the cat looking at?

paintings.why: Officials in wigs and robes gather around a big table in the early government of New France. Charles Huot painted this huge scene of Canadian history, which hangs in the Quebec legislature. It shows how the French colony of Canada was governed in the 1600s. It's a grand history painting.

Instead of horizontal and vertical lines, Theo van Doesburg tilted his grid on the diagonal in 1925, saying it made the picture more dynamic. His friend Piet Mondrian disliked it so much that the two stopped working together.

A waiter in a white uniform stands stiff and serious with his arms at his sides. Soutine painted many hotel workers in Paris, with bold white uniforms in swirling paint. The unusual style makes the plain subject seem important. It's a well-known late portrait.

Gods and goddesses from Japanese legend stand in a misty sky above the sea, creating the islands of Japan with a jeweled spear. Kawamura Kiyoo painted this in a Western oil style, showing the old Shinto myth of the creation of Japan. The story says the god Izanagi and the goddess Izanami stirred the sea with a spear. It's a major painting from Japan's Meiji era.

paintings.t: Portrait of the Kangxi Emperor in Informal Dress Holding a Brush
paintings.why: The Kangxi Emperor sits in a relaxed pose, holding a brush, in a plain robe. The emperor ruled China for 61 years, longer than anyone else, and he painted and wrote poetry as well. This portrait shows him as a scholar, not only a ruler. It's a thoughtful picture of an emperor.

A first sketch for the famous painting of one hundred horses, with horses resting, swimming and playing in a landscape. Giuseppe Castiglione was an Italian missionary and painter who became the court painter of the Chinese emperors. He combined Western realism with Chinese painting. It's a rare look at how he planned a masterpiece.

Sparrows cling to a bending stalk of autumn millet, painted with great care for every feather and seed. Itō Jakuchū was an eccentric Japanese painter in Kyoto who owned a vegetable shop and raised chickens to study them. He is now celebrated as one of Japan's greatest painters of animals. It's a delightful close-up of nature.
paintings.k: How many sparrows can you find? Are any of them hiding?

paintings.t: The Qianlong Emperor's Southern Inspection Tour, Scroll Six: Entering Suzhou along the Grand Canal
paintings.why: A long scroll painting shows the Qianlong Emperor's procession as it travels along a canal, with boats and crowds. Xu Yang was one of the court painters who recorded the tour in a series of giant scrolls. Each scroll is full of details of the landscape and the people. It's a grand record of an imperial journey.

paintings.t: The Qianlong Emperor's Southern Inspection Tour, Scroll Four: The Confluence of the Huai and Yellow Rivers
paintings.why: Another scroll from the series shows the emperor's travels through towns and countryside, with tiny people and boats on the river. Xu Yang painted twelve scrolls about the Qianlong Emperor's tour of southern China. They are among the largest and most detailed pictures from the Qing court. It's a fascinating look at life in 18th-century China.

paintings.t: Moses with the Tablets of the Law
paintings.why: Moses holds the stone tablets of the Ten Commandments, with a calm and strong face. Moritz Daniel Oppenheim, often called the first Jewish painter of modern Germany, painted this early in his career. It was a way of showing Jewish heritage with pride in a time when Jews had few rights. It's an important early work by a pioneer.

paintings.t: A Cloud and Landscape Study by Moonlight
paintings.why: A study of clouds and a landscape in the pale light of the moon. Johan Christian Dahl was among the first painters to study clouds closely, like scientists. He painted them outdoors in quick studies. It's a lovely early example of looking at the sky.
l: Fine Arts Museums of San Francisco

paintings.t: Marriage Portrait of Charlotte de Rothschild
paintings.why: A young bride in a rich wedding gown is shown in a loving portrait. Moritz Daniel Oppenheim was a favorite painter of the Rothschild family, the famous Jewish banking family. He painted it with great care for rich fabrics and jewelry. It's a window into the elegant world of 19th-century Jewish high society.

A group of people gather around a young Shakespeare as he reads aloud a play. Solomon Hart was an English painter and the first Jewish member of the Royal Academy. He painted scenes from history and literature in great detail. It's a warm tribute to the power of storytelling.

paintings.t: Family of General Don Felipe Codallos
paintings.why: A Mexican general, his wife and children pose together in their finest clothes in a formal portrait. Agustín Arrieta was a painter from Puebla, Mexico, who painted portraits and scenes of everyday life. The details of the clothes and furniture are careful. It's a glimpse of Mexican society in 1838.

A young man with an earnest face looks out of the frame. Adolph Tidemand, a Norwegian painter who lived in Düsseldorf, Germany, painted portraits as well as scenes of Norwegian farm life. He helped create the image of Norway's peasants as national heroes. It's an early portrait from his career.
l: National Museum of Art, Architecture and Design

paintings.why: A study of a horse in strong, lively lines. Adolph Tidemand made drawings and paintings of animals as practice for his big pictures of Norwegian life. The horse is full of character. It's a lovely small study.
l: National Museum of Art, Architecture and Design

paintings.t: Milton Visiting Galileo when a Prisoner of the Inquisition
paintings.why: The English poet John Milton visits the aging Italian astronomer Galileo, who is held under house arrest by the Inquisition. Solomon Hart, the first Jewish member of the Royal Academy, painted this scene of two great minds meeting. It celebrates the courage of thinking freely. It's a moving image.

A young woman looks thoughtfully out of the canvas in a quiet, warm portrait. Lida Bendemann was the artist's own relative, painted with careful detail. Eduard Bendemann was a leading German painter. It is a tender portrait of a family member.

paintings.t: Actor Ichikawa Shiko as Kato Yomoshichi
paintings.why: A kabuki actor in a bold costume strikes a dramatic pose in a woodblock print. Konishi Hirosada was a printmaker in Osaka who made prints of famous actors. Fans collected such prints like trading cards. It's a picture of a Japanese theater star.

A lighthouse shines through a night sky on a rough coast, with waves and dark clouds. Peder Balke painted dramatic seascapes of northern Norway in quick, bold strokes. He was little known in his lifetime, but today he is seen as a brilliant artist. It's a moody and powerful picture.
l: National Museum of Art, Architecture and Design

paintings.t: Landscape. Motif from the Numme Valley in Norway
paintings.why: A green valley in the Norwegian mountains, with a river, trees and a farm. Joachim Frich was a Norwegian painter who painted the romantic landscapes of his homeland. He studied in Germany and painted this valley in the 1850s. It's a typical early view of the Norwegian countryside.

Another version of Tidemand's scene of a farmhouse prayer gathering, with a dim room, simple clothing and serious faces. Tidemand painted several versions because the first was so popular. The soft light on the faces and the quiet atmosphere are moving. It's a picture of faith in Norwegian rural life.
l: National Museum of Art, Architecture and Design

paintings.t: Zacharie Vincent et son fils Cyprien
paintings.why: Zacharie Vincent, a Huron-Wendat artist, painted himself and his son, dressed in traditional clothing. He is considered the first Indigenous painter in Quebec, and he signed his work 'the last of the Hurons.' It is a proud self-portrait that shows both identity and strength. It's an important work in Canadian art history.
l: Musée national des beaux-arts du Québec

paintings.t: Lavater and Lessing Visit Moses Mendelssohn
paintings.why: A group of men gather in a study for a friendly but serious debate, with the Jewish philosopher Moses Mendelssohn at the center. Oppenheim painted a famous meeting between Mendelssohn and two Christian thinkers, a story about respect and tolerance. It was an important message for German Jews in the 1800s. It's a famous image in Jewish history.
l: Magnes Collection of Jewish Art and Life

paintings.why: The young shepherd boy Giotto draws a sheep in the dirt as the great painter Cimabue watches in amazement. According to legend, Cimabue saw Giotto's talent and took him as a student. José María Obregón, a Mexican painter, painted this famous story in 1857. It's about discovering a gift.

A young woman lies in the grass above the sea, lost in daydreams. Jozef Israëls, a Dutch painter of Jewish background, was the leader of the Hague School and often painted quiet, thoughtful moments. The soft light and dreamy pose invite you to wonder what she is thinking. It's a gentle picture of imagination.

paintings.t: The Return of the Bear Hunter
paintings.why: A hunter returns home with a bear he's killed, as the family and villagers greet him. Adolph Tidemand painted scenes of Norwegian rural life that were popular across Europe. The hunter is a hero. It's a scene from a harsh but proud way of life.
l: National Museum of Art, Architecture and Design

paintings.why: Big waves crash under a sky of dark clouds in a moody, simple seascape. Peder Balke painted the rough seas of the north with a few strong brushstrokes. His art was forgotten for years, then rediscovered. It's a very modern-looking painting for 1862.

The artist Guadalupe Carpio paints herself with her family, in a warm group portrait. She was one of the first Mexican women to study at the Academy of San Carlos in Mexico City. The picture shows her family around her. It's an unusual self-portrait.

A general with a beard and a serious look stands in uniform. Ulysses S. Grant led the Union army in the American Civil War and later became the 18th president of the United States. This portrait was painted by Ole Peter Hansen Balling, a Norwegian-born painter who fought in the Civil War himself. It's a link between Norway and American history.

A Jewish family rests on the Sabbath in a warm home, with candles and a quiet mood. Moritz Daniel Oppenheim became famous for a series of paintings showing traditional Jewish family life. Many of his pictures were turned into prints and hung in homes across Europe. It's a loving look at a day of rest.

A woman greets her father at the door in a warm, joyful family scene. Maurycy Gottlieb, a Jewish painter from Galicia, studied under the great Polish painter Jan Matejko. He painted this when he was only in his early twenties; he died at 22, but left behind a few remarkable paintings.

A ship finds shelter from a storm at a safe harbor on the Norwegian coast, with a sky of clouds. Hans Gude, a leading Norwegian painter, was a master of ships and the sea. He taught many younger painters in Germany. It's a dramatic coast picture.

Gottlieb, a young Jewish painter, dresses himself as a Polish nobleman, wearing a fur-trimmed coat and a fur hat. He painted this when he was about 20 as a way of saying that Jews were also a part of Polish culture. The proud pose and rich costume are meant to be a statement. It's one of the best-known self-portraits in Polish-Jewish art.
l: Museum of the History of Polish Jews

paintings.why: Jesus speaks to a crowd in Capernaum, with Jewish listeners gathered around him. Maurycy Gottlieb, a Jewish painter, imagined Jesus as a Jewish teacher in a Jewish town. He painted it in the last year of his life. It shows how a Jewish artist could look at a Gospel story as part of his own culture.

Mountains rise over a calm fjord, with the water reflecting the sky and a few boats. Hans Gude painted the grand scenery of Norway, which made him one of the most famous Norwegian painters. The picture shows the beauty of the fjords. It's a classic Norwegian view.

A woman sits alone in a dim room, with her head bowed. Jozef Israëls was a master of painting the loneliness of poor, working people. The few colors and soft light create a deep mood. It's a moving painting from the Hague School.

A cobbler sits and works at his bench in a small shop, surrounded by shoes and tools. Max Liebermann was fascinated by workers and their daily tasks. The warm, gloomy light and the careful composition show his respect for the craft. It's a quiet picture of a simple trade.

The 21st president of the United States, Chester A. Arthur, sits for a formal portrait with a calm, serious expression. Ole Peter Hansen Balling was a Norwegian-born painter who moved to America and painted famous Americans. His portraits tell us how both countries are connected. It's an interesting piece of Norwegian-American art.

A woman sits in a Paris room, with the soft light from a window. Kitty Kielland was one of the first women to become a leading Norwegian landscape painter, and she lived in Paris for a time. This interior shows her skill with light. It's a quiet room scene.
Vasily Polenov, a Russian painter, shows the ruined Parthenon standing high above Athens, the temple Pericles built in the golden age. He visited Greece in the early 1880s and painted it in 1881.

paintings.t: Portrait of the Swedish Painter Karl Nordström
paintings.why: A man with a strong, thoughtful face looks out of a dark background. Christian Krohg, a Norwegian painter, painted his friend Karl Nordström, a Swedish artist. The two met in the artists' colony in Grez-sur-Loing near Paris. It's a portrait of friendship between Nordic artists.
l: National Museum of Art, Architecture and Design

paintings.t: Breakfast I. The Artist's Mother and Brother
paintings.why: A mother and son sit at a simple breakfast table in a warm, bright room. Gustav Wentzel painted this scene of his own family, in a very honest and everyday way. Many Norwegian painters of the 1880s wanted to show real life as it was. It's a cozy and truthful picture.
l: National Museum of Art, Architecture and Design

paintings.why: A woman sits in a dim room, with deep blue shadows and soft, warm light. Harriet Backer was one of Norway's most important painters, and was famous for painting the glow of light inside a room. She taught many younger artists. It's one of the most beautiful pictures of indoor light in Norwegian art.
l: National Museum of Art, Architecture and Design

paintings.why: A mother tenderly holds her baby close in a quiet room. Christian Krohg, a Norwegian painter and writer, often painted mothers and the lives of ordinary women. The soft light shows the love between them. It's a gentle, warm picture.
l: National Museum of Art, Architecture and Design

paintings.why: Families sit at tables under chestnut trees in a Bavarian beer garden, with sunlight shimmering through the leaves. Max Liebermann painted this in Munich and later became the leading German Impressionist. He liked to paint people enjoying leisure. It's a cheerful scene of German life.

Orphan girls sit and walk together in a leafy garden, in the dappled sunshine. This is another version of the orphanage garden theme Max Liebermann loved. He painted it again and again in different lights. It shows his love for the way the light moves through leaves.

A calm Norwegian summer night, with the sun low in a sky of pink and blue and a quiet lake. Kitty Lange Kielland painted the northern light in the midnight summer, when it never gets fully dark. The picture captures a sense of peace. It's a famous Norwegian landscape.
l: National Museum of Art, Architecture and Design

paintings.why: A small stream runs through a snowy landscape, with the blue and white of winter. Frits Thaulow was a Norwegian painter who loved to paint water, in rivers and streams, often in winter. He painted with a pure and clear touch. It's a lovely view of a Norwegian winter.

A woman looks out with a calm, direct gaze in a warm, simple style. Christian Krohg painted his models and friends honestly, in the Realist tradition. He was a leading painter in Norway's art world. It's a lively portrait.
l: National Museum of Art, Architecture and Design

paintings.why: A thoughtful man looks out of the picture. Krøyer painted the English painter Adrian Stokes, a friend he met in Skagen. The picture is a lively, quick sketch. It shows Krøyer's talent for capturing a person's character.

A woman sits in a room lit by a glowing paper lantern, with soft colors. Oda Krohg, a Norwegian painter and a leading figure in the Kristiania bohemians, painted this in 1886. Japanese objects were very fashionable in the 1880s. It's a lovely and modern picture.
l: National Museum of Art, Architecture and Design

paintings.why: Two people sing or play music together in a quiet and cozy room. Peder Severin Krøyer painted scenes of music and friends in Skagen. The warm lamp light is lovely. It's a charming picture.

People wait quietly in a courthouse hall, looking tired and worried. Isidor Kaufmann was a Hungarian Jewish artist who painted Jewish life in Eastern Europe with warmth. This early work shows his talent for painting real people in everyday places. It reminds us how artists record everyday life.

A shoemaker works at his bench in a small farmhouse room, lit by a window. Harriet Backer was one of Norway's greatest painters, famous for the glow of light indoors. She studied in Munich and Paris and later taught many younger artists. The warm light and simple furnishings make an ordinary scene feel special.

A quiet blue night scene with the moon and shimmering water, with few figures. Eilif Peterssen was a Norwegian painter who liked painting history, portraits and mood. Many Norwegian painters in the 1880s painted this kind of atmospheric night. It's a calm and dreamy picture.

paintings.t: Portrait of the Painter Oda Krohg, b. Lasson
paintings.why: A woman in a red blouse stands confidently with her hands on her hips. Oda Krohg was a painter herself and Christian Krohg's wife, and an important figure in the Kristiania art world. Her husband painted her several times. It's a lively tribute from one artist to another.
l: National Museum of Art, Architecture and Design

paintings.why: A large public square in Tehran with people going about their day. Kamal-ol-Molk, the court painter of Iran, painted what he saw with a European realism that was new in Persia. It's an important record of what the city looked like. It's a historical snapshot.

A family sits in a dark house, with a single lamp lighting their faces. Jozef Israëls painted the calm and warmth of simple lives in Dutch homes. The glow of the lamp is gentle. It's a cozy, quiet scene.

A ghostly hunter and his dog lead a pack of spectral figures across a snowy field in a haunting night scene. William Blair Bruce, a Canadian painter from Hamilton, Ontario, painted this in France. It tells an old folk tale about a ghostly hunt. It's a dramatic, spooky picture.

A quiet fjord scene with calm water and mountains in the background. Gunnar Berg was a Norwegian painter who painted the landscapes of northern Norway. The calm water is like a mirror. It's a peaceful picture.
l: National Museum of Art, Architecture and Design

paintings.why: The Bible story in which Abraham is told to offer up his son Isaac, but an angel stops him at the last moment. Yosef Zvi Geiger was an artist born in Jerusalem during the Ottoman era. He painted it in a straightforward, heartfelt way. It's a rare early painting by an artist born in the Holy Land.
A young barefoot girl stands in a sunlit field with her sheep. Paul Peel painted country children in soft light. The peaceful scene was popular in Paris. It's a sweet pastoral picture.

A snowy landscape lit by a pink and gold evening sky, with blue shadows on the snow. Fredrik Borgen was a Norwegian painter who painted the quiet moods of winter. The painting makes the cold feel gentle and calm. It's a beautiful winter view.
l: National Museum of Art, Architecture and Design

paintings.why: A young girl in a fur-trimmed coat and cap looks calmly out of the picture. Erik Werenskiold painted his family and close friends with honesty. He was one of the most respected Norwegian painters and also illustrated Norwegian fairy tales. It's an affectionate family portrait.

A folding fan painted with little portraits of artist friends. Asta Nørregaard, one of Norway's first professional women painters, worked in Kristiania (now Oslo) and was a supporter of other artists. A fan like this was a playful gift to remember friends. It's an unusual and charming piece of art.
l: National Museum of Art, Architecture and Design

paintings.why: A young shepherdess stands in a sunny field in France with her sheep. Suzor-Coté, a Quebec painter, studied in Paris and loved the French countryside. He later painted Canadian winter landscapes. It's an early, gentle picture from his time in France.

Dancers in colorful costume and masks perform the ancient court dance called bugaku, as musicians play. Kanō Eigaku painted the scene in a classic Japanese style with fine details. Bugaku has been performed in Japan for over a thousand years. It's a lively picture of traditional performance.

A group of professors in black robes sit around a table, discussing business, in a group portrait. Max Liebermann was asked to paint the University of Hamburg's professors, and he gave each one a lively, individual look. It shows his gift for capturing character. It's a notable German group portrait.

Visitors stroll and play on the sunny beach at Scheveningen, the seaside resort near The Hague, under a wide sky. Isaac Israëls painted the busy beach with light, quick strokes. The tiny figures and sparkling sand are very lively. It's a happy summer day by the North Sea.

A woman sits at a table in a modern room beside a window with a view of the sea. Léon Bakst was a Jewish artist from Russia, best known for designing amazing costumes and sets for the Ballets Russes in Paris. His sense of color and mood made even simple scenes feel like a stage. This early work shows his stylish touch.

Samuel de Champlain steps off a boat at Quebec in 1608 as he founds the city, while the shoreline is shown behind him. Henri Beau, a Canadian painter, painted this to mark the 300th birthday of Quebec City. It's a scene from the founding of New France. It shows how Canadians remembered their history.
l: Musée national des beaux-arts du Québec

paintings.why: A crowded dance hall in Montmartre in Paris, full of dancing couples and bright lights. Isaac Israëls painted this famous dance garden, which was also painted by Renoir and Van Gogh. His version is quick and full of motion. It's a lively picture of Parisian nightlife.

paintings.t: An Allegorical Wedding- Sketch for a carpet dedicated to Mr. and Mrs. David Wolffsohn Triptych (from...
paintings.why: A colorful design for a carpet, with symbolic figures celebrating a marriage. Ephraim Moses Lilien was a Jewish artist from Galicia, then part of Austria, who designed books, posters and carpets. He was an early artist of the Zionist movement and mixed Art Nouveau style with Jewish themes. It's a good example of how he brought together beauty and tradition.

A vase of autumn flowers sits in a swirl of rich red and golden colors. Léon Bakst used bold, glowing colors that later made his stage designs famous around the world. This picture shows the same love of color in a simple flower vase. It's a colorful decorative picture.

A young woman with a serious look is shown in the rich, graceful style of Léon Bakst, a Jewish Russian artist. Zinaida Gippius was a famous Russian poet and writer in Saint Petersburg, and Bakst painted her as part of the lively circle of artists he belonged to. The portrait shows his skill with line and color. It's a picture of a creative friendship.

paintings.t: Jacques Cartier Meeting the Indians at Stadacona, 1535
paintings.why: The French explorer Jacques Cartier meets the people of Stadacona, a village near what is now Quebec City, in 1535. Suzor-Coté painted the encounter as part of Canada's early history. The picture shows the first contact between French explorers and the Iroquoian people. It's a famous scene in Canadian history.
l: Musée national des beaux-arts du Québec

paintings.why: A giant comet streaks across the night sky over the Mexican landscape. José María Velasco saw the Great Comet of 1882 and painted it. He was a scientist who knew a lot about astronomy. It's a beautiful picture of a real event.
The towers and bridges of Paris are shattered into gray and green slivers, as if you were looking through a prism. Robert Delaunay painted this in 1910, as he was beginning to see color as light.
A flash of lightning cracks over a dark city in Luigi Russolo's painting of 1910. Russolo was a Futurist and also made musical instruments that made the sounds of machines.
A person in a bright orange scarf looks out in a face made of yellow and green patches. Alexej von Jawlensky made this in 1911, when he was painting people in bold, almost wild colors.

Dark blue shapes like folded paper move across the canvas in this abstract pastel made by Arthur Dove in 1911. Dove was an American who lived on a farm and a boat and painted nature as shapes and rhythms.

paintings.t: Windows Open Simultaneously (First Part, Second Motif)
paintings.why: Robert Delaunay painted a window opening onto Paris, but the city dissolves into patches of bright color, like light shining through colored glass. He painted this in 1912 as part of a series of Windows, and a poet called his style Orphism.
The French cathedral town of Laon looks as if it is shaking, with towers tilting in all directions and soft colors. Robert Delaunay painted this in 1912 as he moved toward painting with color alone.

Triangles of yellow, green and brown, like the sails of a boat, fill the painting. Arthur Dove painted this in 1912 to show the feeling of sailing, not just how a boat looks, and he is considered one of the first American abstract painters.

A man in a hat sits and holds his rooster, a fighting cock, ready for a match. Saturnino Herrán painted the ordinary people of Mexico, including farmers and workers, as heroes. The bold shapes show his love of Mexican folk life. It's a proud portrait of a Mexican tradition.
Soft gray shapes, like clouds of smoke, twist and curl in this painting by Arthur Dove, one of the first American abstract painters. He painted music and feelings, and made this one in 1913.

Tom Thomson made this quick sketch for a larger painting of a river in northern Ontario, with rocks and trees in bold color. Thomson was a Canadian painter who spent summers canoeing in Algonquin Park, painting small oil sketches on wooden panels. His fresh, colorful style inspired the Group of Seven. It's a peek at how he began a painting.

Wind-bent trees and rocks stand on the shore of a bright lake, in strong, warm colors. Tom Thomson painted this wild landscape in Algonquin Park. The bold color and thick paint show his modern style. It was one of the paintings that helped make him a Canadian legend.
Overlapping circles and shapes in every color of the rainbow whirl like a carousel or a kaleidoscope. Robert Delaunay painted this in 1915 and wanted color alone to make a kind of music.

A wind-bent pine and a rough lake are painted quickly on a small panel. Tom Thomson made this sketch as a first draft for his masterpiece, 'The West Wind.' You can see how he worked out the wind and the waves. It's a rare look at the first idea for a great painting.

Tall pale houses crowd together like teeth or gravestones in Marsden Hartley's painting of 1916, from a fishing town in Massachusetts. It is part of a series of strange, simple paintings of houses that he called Movements.

A man dressed as a confraternity member for a holy festival, with a serious face and a colorful costume. Saturnino Herrán painted the traditions of Mexican village life with respect. His paintings gave his country pride in its own faces and customs. It's an example of his last works.

A shtetl, a small Jewish town in Eastern Europe, is painted with colorful, geometric shapes. Issachar Ber Ryback was a Ukrainian-born Jewish artist who blended folk art with modern painting. He wanted to keep the memory of Jewish village life alive. It's a bright, modern picture of a vanished world.

A small figure stands in a swirling, wind-blown landscape, painted with thick, twisting strokes. Chaïm Soutine, a Jewish artist from a poor village in Belarus, used paint to express strong feelings instead of copying nature. His landscapes seem to move and twist like they are alive. He painted this in the south of France.

Soutine looks out at us with a serious, uneasy face in thick, quick brushstrokes. He came from a very poor family in a Jewish village in Belarus and was often ill and shy. His self-portraits are bold and emotional. This one is a powerful look at how an artist saw himself.

Houses seem to lean and tumble down a hillside, painted in wavy lines and rich color, as if the earth was shaking. Soutine painted this in the village of Céret in southern France. The buildings seem to dance. It's a dramatic and unforgettable landscape.

A young man with a tilted head and a dazed face is dressed in blue, painted in thick, twisting strokes. Soutine painted many portraits of kitchen workers and ordinary people, and his pictures are full of emotion. The strange title reflects an old and unkind way of describing a person who seemed different. The painting asks us to look carefully at someone others might overlook.

A woman in a dark dress looks out calmly in a quiet portrait. Martin Borgord was a Norwegian painter who lived in Norway and painted portraits and historical scenes. This portrait was painted in 1920. It's an elegant picture of a woman of the era.
Red and purple lollipop-like flowers stand in rows in a magical garden. Paul Klee made this in 1920, mixing plants with architecture, and said a painter should be like a tree, growing up from roots.

paintings.t: Lady in an interior (The artist's wife)
paintings.why: A woman sits in a calm, cozy room, with soft light on her dress. Isidor Kaufmann painted his wife, who was a model for many of his pictures. He is best known for tender pictures of Jewish people in Eastern Europe, and this is a family portrait. It's a loving, quiet picture.

A boy in a white cook's uniform sits stiffly with his hands in his lap, painted in thick white and blue strokes. Soutine painted waiters, cooks and bellboys in Paris, with strong, emotional style. The wavy lines make the white clothes look almost alive. It's one of his best-known portraits.
Two dancing orange figures stand in front of a dark background with the roman numeral V. Paul Klee made this playful picture in 1922 and it looks a bit like a family of flowers.

A large rayfish hangs against a dark background with a bowl and bottles, painted with wild, swirling strokes. Soutine was inspired by famous Dutch still lifes of fish and meat but gave them a more emotional twist. The fish seems to swim in the air. It's among his famous still lifes.

Rows of tall, plain houses stand in a coal town in Cape Breton, Nova Scotia, with smoke and snow. Lawren Harris, a member of the Group of Seven, painted this in 1925, using strong, simple shapes. He wanted to show the dignity of working people in Canadian life. It's an iconic painting of Canada's industrial past.

paintings.t: Red Circle on a Black Surface
paintings.why: A bright red circle floats on a black ground with a tiny white bar underneath like a spaceship. Ilya Chashnik, a student of Malevich, made this around 1925.
A single golden fish glows in a dark blue sea full of red fish in Paul Klee's picture of 1925. It looks as if it's swimming through a dream, and it is one of Klee's best-loved pictures.
A little fleet of boats in red, blue and green sits under a red sun in a harbor made of triangles. Paul Klee painted this in 1927, and the simple shapes make it look like a toy box.
A grid of pale lines grows from a little building shape, step by step, like a game. Klee made it in 1927 to show how a simple idea can grow into something complicated.
Dark red teardrop shapes and strange little pictures hang like tools in a puzzle, in Paul Klee's Omega 5 of 1927. It's like a story in code.

A fashionable woman in a red dress sits in a chair against a swirling background. Madeleine Castaing was a Paris patron and collector who supported Soutine and bought many of his works. Soutine painted her in bold colors with a lively brush. It's a portrait of a friend who helped him succeed.
A big orange sun rises over soft green hills and a quiet harbor on Long Island in Arthur Dove's painting of 1929. Dove simplified nature into smooth, calm shapes.
A funny little jester with a spiky hat and bendy arms is lost in a dream. Paul Klee painted this in 1929 on fine pale paper, and made a whole circus of such creatures.

paintings.t: Empress Zoe and Constantine IX, Hagia Sophia
paintings.why: In a golden mosaic in the church of Hagia Sophia, the Byzantine Empress Zoe and her husband Constantine IX stand on each side of Christ and offer gifts. It was made in the 1000s, when Constantinople was one of the richest cities on Earth.

Harold, the last Anglo-Saxon king of England, dies at the Battle of Hastings in 1066. The Bayeux Tapestry, an embroidered strip about 70 meters long, tells the story of the Norman conquest in stitches, and tradition says Harold was killed by an arrow in the eye.

paintings.t: Norman Knights and Archers at Hastings (Bayeux Tapestry)
paintings.why: Norman knights on horses and archers charge in this section of the Bayeux Tapestry, the embroidered story of the conquest of England in 1066. It was made only a few years later, so the artists were close to the events.
Harold takes the throne of England in January 1066 after King Edward dies, in a scene from the Bayeux Tapestry. William of Normandy said the crown was promised to him, which led to the invasion.

paintings.t: Harold Swears an Oath to William (Bayeux Tapestry)
paintings.why: Harold swears an oath of loyalty to William of Normandy with his hands on holy relics, in a scene from the Bayeux Tapestry. The Normans later said that Harold broke this promise when he became king.
The Bayeux Tapestry begins with the old, childless King Edward the Confessor of England on his throne, whose death would lead to the fight for the crown in 1066.

paintings.t: Horses in the Battle of Hastings (Bayeux Tapestry)
paintings.why: Horses tumble and soldiers fight at the Battle of Hastings in the Bayeux Tapestry. The embroidery is a strip of linen stitched with colored wool in the 1070s, and it is one of the world's most famous works of medieval art.
William of Normandy gives Harold weapons in this scene from the Bayeux Tapestry. Medieval viewers could read the Latin words stitched above the figures, which act like captions.

paintings.t: Bishop Odo, William and Robert (Bayeux Tapestry)
paintings.why: Duke William of Normandy sits with his half-brothers, Bishop Odo and Robert, planning the invasion of England. Odo is thought to have ordered the Bayeux Tapestry to be made.

The Virgin Mary and Child with the Emperor John II Komnenos and the Empress Irene, in a glittering golden mosaic in Hagia Sophia made around 1118. Byzantine emperors liked to show themselves offering gifts to holy figures.

paintings.t: Henry VI Pardons Richard the Lionheart
paintings.why: After the Third Crusade, Richard the Lionheart was captured on his way home and held for ransom by the Holy Roman Emperor Henry VI, who finally pardoned him. This drawing comes from a book made for the emperor around 1196 by Peter of Eboli.

Saladin, the great Muslim leader who recaptured Jerusalem in 1187, meets Guy of Lusignan, the king of Jerusalem he had defeated at Hattin. The English monk Matthew Paris drew this lively sketch around 1250.

Christ looks out from the Deësis mosaic of Hagia Sophia, with the Virgin Mary and John the Baptist on either side. It was probably made around 1261, when the Byzantines recaptured Constantinople, and is thought to be one of the finest mosaics in the world.

paintings.t: Emperor Frederick II Meets Sultan al-Kamil
paintings.why: In 1229 Emperor Frederick II made a treaty with Sultan al-Kamil of Egypt, which gave Jerusalem back to the Christians without a battle. This picture comes from the Nuova Cronica of Giovanni Villani, a 14th-century chronicle of Florence.
Master Theodoric, the court painter to Emperor Charles IV in Prague, painted Charlemagne as a saint in the 1360s. Charles IV, who was named for Charlemagne, admired his great predecessor.

The emperor Charlemagne and his son Louis the Pious stand side by side in a manuscript illumination from a French royal chronicle of the 1300s or 1400s. Louis became emperor after Charlemagne died in 814.

paintings.t: The Battle of Agincourt (St Albans Chronicle)
paintings.why: This medieval chronicle picture of the Battle of Agincourt in 1415 was painted only a few years after the battle itself, in the chronicle of the monk Thomas Walsingham. English longbowmen shot down the charging French knights.

The hero Roland, one of Charlemagne's knights, dies after fighting at Roncesvalles in 778, in the legend that became the Song of Roland. Jean Fouquet painted it in a French royal manuscript around 1455.

Ottoman ships crowd the water around the walled city of Constantinople in this manuscript painting of the siege of 1453. Jean Le Tavernier painted it for a Burgundian duke only a few years after the city fell.

paintings.t: The Coronation of Charlemagne (Grandes Chroniques de France)
paintings.why: This glowing little picture of Charlemagne's crowning comes from the Grandes Chroniques de France, the French royal history. Jean Fouquet, the court painter, made it around 1458.

paintings.t: The Building of the Chapel at Aachen (Grandes Chroniques de France)
paintings.why: Workers build the great chapel at Aachen, Charlemagne's capital, using ladders and stone blocks. The scene is from the Grandes Chroniques de France, illustrated by Jean Fouquet around 1458.

Ottoman soldiers with ladders and cannon storm the walls in this French manuscript painting of the fall of Constantinople in 1453, made only a few years afterward. Philippe de Mazerolles painted it around 1460.

A long Renaissance chest-panel shows the Battle of Zama in 202 BC, where Scipio finally beat Hannibal and ended the Second Punic War. The artist is known only as the Master of the Battle of Anghiari, and the painting was made around 1470.

paintings.t: The Conquest of Constantinople by the Crusaders in 1204
paintings.why: In 1204 crusaders on the Fourth Crusade attacked the Christian city of Constantinople from their ships instead of going to the Holy Land. This French manuscript painting was made around 1470 and shows them swarming the walls.

English longbowmen face French knights and crossbowmen in a colorful scene from the chronicles of Jean Froissart, the great historian of the Hundred Years' War. It was painted around 1470 in a richly decorated manuscript.
In 1095 Pope Urban II gives a famous speech at Clermont that started the First Crusade, and the crowd shouts 'God wills it!' This illustration comes from a French manuscript made around 1474.

Botticelli painted the Three Kings visiting Jesus and gave the kings the faces of the Medici family, the rulers of Florence, and put himself in the crowd. He painted it around 1475, a glimpse of how rich Renaissance patrons liked to be shown.

Mehmed II conquered Constantinople in 1453 when he was only 21, and later he asked Venice to send a painter to his court. Gentile Bellini painted this portrait of the sultan in 1480 and framed him in a fancy arch.

A walled city is attacked with cannons and ladders in this illuminated manuscript showing the siege of Orléans in 1428–1429, the turning point of the Hundred Years' War. It was painted around 1484 in a chronicle of King Charles VII.

The goddess Venus arrives on the shore on a giant seashell, blown by the winds, in Botticelli's most famous painting of about 1485. It was made for the Medici family of Florence and shows how Renaissance artists were reviving ancient myths.

A long painted frieze shows skeletons leading people of every rank in a dance toward the grave. Bernt Notke made it around 1490 for a church in Tallinn, in the years when plague and death were never far from people's thoughts.

Skeletons lead a long line of kings, bishops, merchants and peasants toward the grave in this wall painting in a tiny church in Slovenia. John of Kastav painted it in 1490 in the years after the Black Death, when the Dance of Death was a favorite subject.

A young woman, Cecilia Gallerani, holds a white ermine, which was a symbol of purity, in one of Leonardo's few portraits of a woman. He painted it in about 1490 for the court of Milan, and the way she turns her head makes the picture feel alive.

Leonardo's famous drawing of a man with arms and legs stretched inside a circle and a square shows the ideal human proportions described by the Roman architect Vitruvius. It captures the Renaissance idea that humans are the center of the universe, and the drawing is about 1490.
Skeletons dance with the living in this woodcut from the Nuremberg Chronicle of 1493. The Dance of Death, popular after the Black Death, reminded everyone that death comes for rich and poor alike.

paintings.t: Saint Sebastian Interceding for the Plague Victims
paintings.why: People in a plague-struck city pray to Saint Sebastian, who was believed to protect against the disease, while angels and demons hover above. Josse Lieferinxe painted this scene around 1497.

Leonardo painted the moment Jesus tells his twelve friends that one of them will betray him, and each gesture shows a different reaction. He painted it on a wall in Milan in about 1495–1498 and used perspective to draw every line toward Jesus.

Girolamo Savonarola was a fiery preacher who held Florence in his grip in the 1490s, burning books, mirrors and paintings in his Bonfire of the Vanities. His friend, the painter Fra Bartolomeo, painted him in 1498, the year he was executed.

Girolamo Savonarola, the preacher who ruled Florence for a few years, is hanged and burned in the main square in 1498 after losing the support of the people. This painting was made not long after, and shows the whole square from above.
Clovis, the king of the Franks, is baptized by a bishop around the year 496, which made France a Christian kingdom. The painter, known only as the Master of Saint Giles, made this panel around 1500.

The Mona Lisa's soft, mysterious smile and misty background make her the most famous painting in the world. Leonardo da Vinci worked on it from around 1503 and kept it with him until he died; today it hangs in the Louvre, where millions come to see it.
Giovanni Bellini painted this long, stone-colored picture around 1506 to look like an ancient Roman carved frieze, telling a story of Scipio's mercy.

Raphael filled a Vatican room with the great thinkers of ancient Greece: Plato points up at the sky of ideas while Aristotle holds out a hand toward the Earth. Painted around 1511 at the height of the Italian Renaissance, it says that the new age was a rebirth of the clear thinking of ancient Athens.

God stretches out a finger toward Adam, and the tiny gap between their hands has become one of the most famous images ever. Michelangelo painted it in 1512 as part of the ceiling of the Sistine Chapel.

paintings.t: The Meeting of Leo the Great and Attila
paintings.why: In 452 Pope Leo I met Attila the Hun and, according to the story, persuaded him to turn his army back from Rome. Raphael painted the legend in the Vatican in 1514, with the apostles Peter and Paul appearing in the sky.
On Christmas Day in 800, Pope Leo III crowns Charlemagne emperor in Rome, the first emperor in the West in over 300 years. Raphael painted this ceremony in the Vatican around 1516, centuries later.

Cosimo de' Medici the Elder was the banker who made his family the rulers of Florence, and he paid for libraries, churches and artists. Pontormo painted this portrait around 1519, 55 years after Cosimo died.

paintings.t: Portrait of a Man, Said to Be Christopher Columbus
paintings.why: This famous portrait is said to show Christopher Columbus, but it was painted by Sebastiano del Piombo in 1519, years after Columbus died, and no one knows what the explorer really looked like.

paintings.t: The Battle of the Milvian Bridge
paintings.why: Constantine's army defeats his rival Maxentius at the Milvian Bridge in 312 AD, a victory he said was helped by a vision of a cross. Giulio Romano painted this big battle in the Vatican around 1520.

Erasmus, the Dutch scholar who wrote with wit about the Church's faults, sits writing in this calm portrait by Hans Holbein the Younger of 1523. Erasmus wanted to reform the Church from inside and never joined Luther.
Philipp Melanchthon, the teacher and thinker who became Luther's closest partner in the Reformation, in an engraving by Albrecht Dürer from 1526. Dürer admired Luther's cause.

Martin Luther, the monk who challenged the Church, in a portrait painted in 1528 by his friend Lucas Cranach the Elder. Cranach painted Luther many times, and his portraits helped spread Luther's face across Europe.

paintings.t: The Battle of Alexander at Issus
paintings.why: Thousands of tiny soldiers swarm across a landscape of mountains, sea and glowing sky in Albrecht Altdorfer's view of Alexander the Great beating the Persian king Darius at Issus in 333 BC. He painted it in 1529 for a duke of Bavaria and made it feel like a whole world, not just a battle.

Thomas Cromwell, Henry VIII's chief minister, carried out the king's break with Rome and closed England's monasteries, but he fell from power and was executed in 1540. Holbein painted him in 1533 at the height of his influence.

The Virgin Mary spreads her cloak over sailors, explorers and ships in an altarpiece painted for the Spanish House of Trade in Seville in about 1535. Christopher Columbus is thought to appear among the kneeling figures, and it is one of the first paintings to show the Americas.

Henry VIII, in a puffed gold and jeweled jacket, stands with his hands on his hips in this Holbein portrait of 1537. Henry broke with the pope in the 1530s to marry Anne Boleyn and made himself head of the Church of England.

paintings.t: The Dance of Death: The Emperor
paintings.why: Death, a skeleton, leads the emperor away from his throne in one of Hans Holbein the Younger's Dance of Death woodcuts. The series, made in the 1520s and 1530s, warned that nobody, not even an emperor, can escape.

paintings.t: The Dance of Death: The Cardinal
paintings.why: A skeleton gently takes a cardinal by the robe in one of Holbein's Dance of Death woodcuts. The pictures were often both frightening and funny, and they were very popular after the Black Death.

paintings.t: Portraits of Martin Luther and Philipp Melanchthon
paintings.why: Martin Luther and his friend and fellow reformer Philipp Melanchthon, shown side by side in two matching panels painted by Lucas Cranach the Elder in 1543. Melanchthon was the scholar who organized Luther's ideas.
Pope Paul III, the pope who called the Council of Trent and approved the new Jesuit order, in a portrait painted by Titian in 1543. He led the Catholic response to the Reformation.

Thomas Cranmer, the Archbishop of Canterbury who helped Henry VIII break with Rome and wrote the English Book of Common Prayer, was burned at the stake in 1556 under Queen Mary. Gerlach Flicke painted this portrait in 1545.

paintings.t: The Field of the Cloth of Gold
paintings.why: In 1520 King Henry VIII of England and King Francis I of France met near Calais in a huge display of tents, banquets and tournaments, each trying to look richer than the other. This painting of about 1545 shows the festival soon after Henry and the pope split apart, when the age of Catholic Europe was ending.
Philip II, King of Spain, as a young prince in glittering armor and white hose. Titian painted him in 1551, and Philip later married Queen Mary I of England and sent the Armada against Elizabeth.

The Dutch painter Maarten van Heemskerck shows himself in front of the Colosseum in 1553, when the great arena was already a crumbling ruin. It is one of the first pictures to treat Roman ruins as something precious.

Mary I, queen of England from 1553 to 1558, tried to bring England back to the Catholic Church and was nicknamed 'Bloody Mary' by her enemies. Antonis Mor painted her in 1554, the year she married Philip of Spain.
Mary, Queen of Scots, was Elizabeth I's cousin and rival, held prisoner in England for 19 years before she was beheaded in 1587. This small portrait shows her in the 1560s.

An army of skeletons sweeps across a ruined land, killing kings and peasants alike. Pieter Bruegel the Elder painted it around 1562, and it echoes the horror of the Black Death and other plagues that swept over Europe.
A crowded engraving of the Battle of Zama, where Scipio defeated Hannibal in 202 BC. Cornelis Cort made it in 1567 from a Renaissance design, and prints like this spread famous stories across Europe.

paintings.t: The Family of Darius before Alexander
paintings.why: After the Battle of Issus, the mother and family of the defeated Persian king kneel before Alexander. The queen mother bows to Alexander's friend Hephaestion by mistake, and Alexander kindly says he is Alexander too. Paolo Veronese painted this story of mercy around 1570.

Jacopo Tintoretto paints the Venetians and crusaders capturing Constantinople in 1204 as a dark swirl of fighting. He made it in the 1580s for the Doge's Palace in Venice, which took pride in the event.

Bishops fill a great hall at the Council of Trent, held between 1545 and 1563 to answer the Protestant Reformation and reform the Catholic Church. Pasquale Cati painted this view of the council in 1588.

paintings.t: The Armada Portrait of Elizabeth I
paintings.why: Queen Elizabeth I rests her hand on a globe, a symbol that she ruled the seas, while behind her are scenes of the Spanish Armada's defeat in 1588. This is the most famous portrait of an English queen and was painted to celebrate the victory.

The explorer Amerigo Vespucci stands in front of a woman who stands for America, newly awakened, in an allegorical engraving by Stradanus of about 1589. The continents were named for Vespucci's first name.

Sir Francis Walsingham, Elizabeth I's spymaster, uncovered plots against the queen, including the one that led to the downfall of Mary, Queen of Scots. John de Critz painted this portrait of him in 1589, near the time of the Armada.
Niccolò Machiavelli was a Florentine thinker who wrote The Prince, a book about how rulers really get and keep power. Santi di Tito painted this famous portrait of him about 60 years after his death.

paintings.t: English Ships and the Spanish Armada, August 1588
paintings.why: A crowd of English and Spanish ships sail in the crescent formation of the Spanish Armada in this painting made not long after the battle of 1588. It is one of the earliest pictures of the event.
Francis Drake rests his hand on a globe in a portrait celebrating his voyage around the world from 1577 to 1580, the first by an English captain. Marcus Gheeraerts the Younger painted it in 1591.
Elizabeth I in a huge white ruff and jeweled gown, painted around 1595 by Marcus Gheeraerts the Younger. Portraits of Elizabeth were made carefully to make the queen look powerful and never old.

paintings.t: Namban Screen: The Arrival of the Portuguese
paintings.why: A huge Portuguese trading ship sails into a golden Japanese harbor, with people in strange foreign clothes. These folding screens, called Namban, or 'southern barbarian' screens, showed how Japanese people saw the first Europeans, who arrived in 1543. Kanō Naizen painted this one around 1600.

paintings.t: Prince Maurice at the Battle of Nieuwpoort, 1600
paintings.why: Prince Maurice of Orange leads on a white horse at the Battle of Nieuwpoort in 1600, a big Dutch victory over the Spanish in the fight for independence. The painting was made later, in the 1800s.

paintings.t: The Procession Portrait of Elizabeth I
paintings.why: Elizabeth I is carried in a grand procession by her courtiers and noblemen, like the center of a parade. This portrait from about 1601 shows how splendid her court was in her last years.

Jan Brueghel the Elder spreads thousands of tiny soldiers across a sunlit plain for the battle that ended the Persian Empire, probably Alexander's win over King Darius. Painted in 1602, it is full of little details to hunt for.

paintings.t: The Rainbow Portrait of Elizabeth I
paintings.why: Elizabeth I, about 70 years old, holds a rainbow and wears a cloak covered in eyes and ears, a symbol of how much she saw. The painting from around 1602 shows her as ageless and wise, as she wished to be remembered.

According to Roman legend, the twin babies Romulus and Remus were left by a river and fed by a she-wolf until a shepherd found them. Peter Paul Rubens painted this origin story of Rome around 1615, with the river god Tiber looking on.

In 390 Bishop Ambrose of Milan stands in the church doorway and refuses to let the Emperor Theodosius enter until he repents for a terrible massacre. The story shows the Church becoming powerful enough to stand up to emperors. Rubens painted it in 1617 and Van Dyck made this version soon after.

paintings.t: Dutch Ships Ramming Spanish Galleys off the Flemish Coast
paintings.why: A tall Dutch warship rams Spanish galleys off the coast of Flanders in a battle of the long Dutch fight for independence from Spain. Hendrick Cornelisz. Vroom, the first great Dutch painter of ships, painted it in 1617.

paintings.t: The Triumphant Entry of Constantine into Rome
paintings.why: The emperor Constantine rides into Rome in 312 AD after beating his rival at the Milvian Bridge, an event that opened the way for Christianity to become the empire's main religion. Peter Paul Rubens designed the scene in 1621 as part of a tapestry series.

paintings.t: Constantius Appoints Constantine as His Successor
paintings.why: Constantius, a Roman emperor, names his son Constantine as his successor in 306 AD, and Constantine goes on to become the first Christian emperor. Peter Paul Rubens painted this scene in 1622 for a series about Constantine's life.

Alexander the Great, who has everything, offers the philosopher Diogenes anything he wants. Diogenes, lying in the sun, just asks him to stop blocking the light. Gaspar de Crayer painted this meeting in the 1620s.

A young Roman woman named Cloelia, held hostage by the Etruscan king Porsena, escapes and leads other hostages across the Tiber river. Peter Paul Rubens painted the daring escape with his usual energy and glowing skin tones.

Rioters climb ladders to smash saints' statues and stained glass inside a church, as Protestants did during the Dutch Revolt of the 1500s. Dirck van Delen painted this scene of church-breaking in 1630.

paintings.t: The Rape of the Sabine Women
paintings.why: In Roman legend the young city of Rome had no wives, so Romulus's men carried off the women of the neighboring Sabine tribe. Nicolas Poussin painted this chaotic scene in 1634 in his calm, classical style.

The Dutch governor hands the keys of the city of Breda to the Spanish general Spinola in 1625, and Spinola kindly stops him from kneeling. Diego Velázquez painted it around 1635 and the forest of spears gave it the nickname Las Lanzas.

In 1620 the Catholic army defeated the Protestant Bohemian forces outside Prague on the White Mountain, an early victory in the Thirty Years' War. Peter Snayers painted the whole sweeping battlefield.

Anthony van Dyck painted the face of King Charles I from three sides in 1635 so that the sculptor Bernini in Rome could carve a bust of the king from the picture. It is one of the most famous portraits of an English king.

King Charles I rides a gray horse in a grand portrait by Anthony van Dyck of about 1637. Van Dyck, the king's court painter, made the short king look tall and noble, and the portrait shows the style of rule that led to the civil war.

paintings.t: The Five Eldest Children of Charles I
paintings.why: The five eldest children of Charles I, including the future kings Charles II and James II, stand with a huge dog in one of the sweetest royal portraits. Anthony van Dyck painted it in 1637, only a few years before the family was torn apart by civil war.

paintings.t: The Destruction of the Temple at Jerusalem
paintings.why: In AD 70 the Roman army under the future emperor Titus destroyed the Temple in Jerusalem at the end of a Jewish revolt. Nicolas Poussin painted this violent scene in 1638.

paintings.t: Before the Battle of the Downs
paintings.why: Dutch and Spanish fleets face each other before the Battle of the Downs in 1639, where the Dutch admiral Tromp destroyed a Spanish fleet off the English coast. Reinier Nooms painted it around that year.
The same story of fairness in war: Scipio hands a captive woman back to her fiancé. Nicolas Poussin painted it around 1640 with the careful, classical order that he was known for.

Claude Lorrain turns the arrival of Cleopatra at Tarsus into a glowing harbor scene, where the Egyptian queen steps ashore to meet Mark Antony in the golden light of sunrise. Painted in 1642, it is more about light on water than about the story.
Armies clash across a wide plain at the Battle of Lützen in 1632, where the Swedish king Gustavus Adolphus won the battle but was killed. Peter Snayers painted it in 1642.
The legendary Roman soldier Horatius Cocles holds a bridge alone against an enemy army while his friends chop it down behind him. Charles Le Brun painted the story of early Roman courage around 1642.

paintings.t: Romulus and Remus Sheltered by Faustulus
paintings.why: A shepherd family takes in the twin babies who will one day found Rome, in a calm, sunlit scene full of warm colors. Pietro da Cortona painted it in 1643.

paintings.t: The Ratification of the Treaty of Münster
paintings.why: Delegates from Spain and the Dutch Republic raise their hands to swear to the peace treaty of 1648 that ended the Eighty Years' War. Gerard ter Borch, who was there, painted it as a group of tiny, lifelike portraits.

paintings.t: Banquet of the Amsterdam Civic Guard in Celebration of the Treaty of Münster
paintings.why: Members of Amsterdam's civic guard celebrate the Peace of Münster in 1648 at an enormous feast, a group portrait of dozens of men in their Sunday best. Bartholomeus van der Helst painted it in the year peace came.

Oliver Cromwell, the commander of the Parliament's army in the English Civil War, stands in armor with a young page beside him. Robert Walker painted him in 1649, the year the king was executed, and Cromwell later ruled England as Lord Protector.

paintings.t: The Execution of King Charles I
paintings.why: A crowd gathers outside the Banqueting House in London on January 30, 1649, where King Charles I was beheaded, the only time an English king was executed. This print was made around the time of the event.

paintings.t: The Battle of Alexander against Darius
paintings.why: Pietro da Cortona paints a whirlwind of horses and spears as Alexander charges at the Persian king Darius. Painted in the 1600s for a Roman family, it treats an ancient victory as an energetic Baroque spectacle.

A terrible illness has struck an ancient city and people are dying in the streets. Michiel Sweerts painted it around 1652 and it is often connected to the plague that hit Athens in 430 BC during the long war with Sparta, an event that shook the golden age.

paintings.t: Aristotle with a Bust of Homer
paintings.why: The philosopher Aristotle, dressed in rich 1600s clothes, rests a hand on a bust of the poet Homer and seems lost in thought about wisdom, fame and money. Rembrandt painted it in 1653, and it is one of the most famous pictures of a thinker in all of art.

Cleopatra bets Mark Antony that she can spend a fortune on one dinner, then drops a priceless pearl in her wine and drinks it. Jacob Jordaens shows the crowded feast in his lively Flemish style in 1653.

paintings.t: The Shepherd Faustulus Bringing Romulus and Remus to His Wife
paintings.why: The shepherd Faustulus brings the two baby twins, found beside the wolf, home to his wife to raise. In Roman legend they grew up to found the city of Rome. Nicolas Mignard painted this tender scene in 1654.

paintings.t: Allegory of the Peace of Westphalia
paintings.why: Jacob Jordaens fills a canvas with gods, figures and symbols of peace to celebrate the Peace of Westphalia, the treaties of 1648 that ended the Thirty Years' War. He painted it in 1654.

paintings.t: Doctor Schnabel of Rome (a plague doctor)
paintings.why: A plague doctor wears a long coat and a mask with a beak that was stuffed with herbs, to try to keep disease away. This engraving of 1656 shows one in Rome, and the beaked doctor is now one of the most famous images of the plague.

An army attacks the German city of Magdeburg in 1631, one of the worst moments of the Thirty Years' War, when most of the city was destroyed. This engraving was made in the workshop of Matthäus Merian.

Lucretia, a noble Roman woman, stands with a dagger after a terrible wrong, and according to legend her death made the Romans drive out their last king in 509 BC and create the Republic. Rembrandt painted her thoughtful face in 1664, near the end of his life.
This watercolor shows the small Dutch town of New Amsterdam on the tip of Manhattan, with windmills, ships and a fort. It was drawn in 1664, the year the English took it over and renamed it New York.

paintings.t: The Entry of Alexander into Babylon
paintings.why: Alexander rides into Babylon on a chariot in 331 BC with elephants, flower petals and cheering crowds. Charles Le Brun painted this for King Louis XIV of France, who loved being compared to Alexander.

Alexander's cavalry charges across the Granicus river in 334 BC, the first big battle against the Persians. It is the first of five huge paintings Charles Le Brun made for Louis XIV about Alexander's victories.

Charles II, who was brought back as king in 1660 after eleven years without a monarch, sits in elegant robes. This portrait was painted around 1665 by John Michael Wright, and Charles was known as the Merry Monarch.

paintings.t: Louis XIV Visiting the Royal Academy of Sciences
paintings.why: King Louis XIV visits the Royal Academy of Sciences in Paris in 1671, where telescopes, globes and instruments show how science was becoming an official part of French life. This engraving was made by Sébastien Leclerc in the same year.

Dozens of oared warships crash together at Actium in 31 BC, the sea battle where Octavian's fleet beat Mark Antony and Cleopatra. After it Octavian became Augustus, the first Roman emperor. Laureys a Castro painted it in 1672.

The Indian king Porus, who fought bravely and lost, is brought before Alexander. Alexander asks how he wants to be treated and Porus answers, like a king, and Alexander lets him keep his kingdom. Charles Le Brun painted the scene in 1673.

In July 1690 the Protestant King William III defeated the Catholic King James II at the Battle of the Boyne in Ireland, ending James's hope of getting back his throne. Jan van Huchtenburgh painted this crowded battle in the 1690s.

paintings.t: Peter the Great, Tsar of Russia (1672-1725)
paintings.why: Peter the Great, in armor, painted by Godfrey Kneller in 1698 while Peter was visiting England to learn about shipbuilding. The young tsar traveled in Europe to bring new ideas back to Russia.

Julius Caesar, stabbed by senators on the Ides of March in 44 BC, falls at the foot of the statue of his old rival Pompey. Victor Honoré Janssens, a Flemish painter, painted this version of the assassination around 1700.
Sir Isaac Newton, who explained gravity and the movement of the planets, looks out of this portrait by Godfrey Kneller from 1702. Newton's ideas were a cornerstone of the Enlightenment.
A French painter at Peter's court, Pierre-Denis Martin, painted this view of the Battle of Poltava in 1726, only 17 years after it happened. It shows the whole plain with its lines of soldiers.

paintings.t: The Capture of the Alcide and Lys near Louisbourg, 1755
paintings.why: British warships capture the French ships Alcide and Lys off the coast of Canada in 1755, in the sea fight that helped start the Seven Years' War.
Alexander the Great sits with Roxane, the Bactrian princess he married in 327 BC. Pietro Rotari painted this gentle scene in 1756 as a romantic story from the life of the famous conqueror.

paintings.t: A View of the Plundering and Burning of the City of Grimross
paintings.why: British ships and soldiers burn an Acadian settlement on the Saint John River in 1758, during the Seven Years' War. The engraving after the soldier-artist Thomas Davies shows smoke hanging over the water.

paintings.t: Lord Clive Meeting Mir Jafar after the Battle of Plassey
paintings.why: After the Battle of Plassey in 1757, Robert Clive of the East India Company meets Mir Jafar, the Indian ruler he helped put in power, in a scene from the global Seven Years' War. Francis Hayman painted it around 1760.

paintings.t: Colonel Bouquet and the Return of Captives, 1764
paintings.why: After Pontiac's War, Colonel Henry Bouquet forced the Native nations to hand back the settlers they had taken, and many of the captives, who had grown up with Native families, did not want to leave. This engraving, after Benjamin West, appeared in 1766.
According to legend, whoever could untie the huge Gordian knot would rule Asia. Alexander drew his sword and cut straight through it. Jean-Simon Berthélemy painted this clever solution in 1767.
The silversmith Paul Revere, later famous for his midnight ride in 1775, rests his chin on his hand in front of a gleaming teapot. John Singleton Copley painted him at work in 1768.

The boy Hannibal swears at an altar to hate Rome forever, with his father Hamilcar watching. Benjamin West painted it in 1770 while visiting Rome as a young American artist, and later George III bought it.

paintings.t: The Bloody Massacre Perpetrated in King Street Boston
paintings.why: British soldiers fire into a crowd in Boston on March 5, 1770, killing five colonists. Paul Revere copied and published this engraving, which made the Boston Massacre famous and helped turn many colonists against Britain.

paintings.t: The Burning of the Prudent and Capture of the Bienfaisant at Louisbourg
paintings.why: British sailors set fire to the French warship Prudent in the harbor of Louisbourg in 1758, when the British captured the fortress, a key step toward taking Quebec. This engraving was published in 1771.

At the front of the great French Encyclopédie, Truth is unveiled by Reason and Philosophy, with the light of knowledge shining. The Encyclopédie, edited by Diderot, gathered all the Enlightenment's knowledge, and this engraving by Charles-Nicolas Cochin was its frontispiece in 1772.

paintings.t: George Washington as a Virginia Colonel
paintings.why: George Washington, in the red and blue uniform of a Virginia militia colonel, in a portrait painted in 1772 by Charles Willson Peale. Washington had fought in the French and Indian War, the American part of the Seven Years' War.

paintings.t: The Death of Paulus Aemilius at the Battle of Cannae
paintings.why: At the Battle of Cannae in 216 BC, Hannibal's army surrounded and crushed a larger Roman army, one of the greatest defeats in Roman history. John Trumbull painted this scene of the dying Roman consul Paulus Aemilius in 1773 as an early work.

Denis Diderot, the editor of the Encyclopédie, which tried to collect all of human knowledge in one set of books. Dmitry Levitzky painted him in 1773, when Catherine the Great invited the philosopher to Russia.

paintings.t: Alcibiades Receiving a Lesson from Socrates
paintings.why: The philosopher Socrates teaches the young Alcibiades, a brilliant and very spoiled Athenian aristocrat who later became a famous general and then a traitor. François-André Vincent painted it in 1776, when French artists were turning to stories of ancient Greece and Rome.

Belisarius, the great general of the Byzantine emperor Justinian, is said in a legend to have ended his life blind and begging, and here a soldier who once served under him recognizes him. Jacques-Louis David painted it in 1781, and it made him famous.

Miltiades, the Athenian general who won at Marathon, died in disgrace, and his son Cimon agreed to take his place in prison so that his father could have a proper funeral. Jean-François Pierre Peyron painted this story of loyalty in 1782 for the Paris Salon.

Hubert Robert paints the Great Fire of Rome in AD 64 with a river-bridge silhouetted against the flames. According to Roman writers, Nero blamed the Christians, though many people thought he started it himself.
Benjamin Franklin, scientist, printer and American diplomat, in a portrait painted in Paris in 1785 by Joseph-Siffred Duplessis. It is the portrait that was later used for the US hundred-dollar bill.

The Roman general Marius, hiding from enemies in a marsh, stares down the soldier sent to kill him, who drops his sword. Jean Germain Drouais painted this tense moment from the civil wars before Caesar in 1786.

On June 17, 1775, British troops stormed Bunker Hill outside Boston, one of the first big battles of the American Revolution, and the American general Joseph Warren was killed. John Trumbull, who watched the battle from across the river, painted it in 1786.

Queen Marie Antoinette sits with her children in a portrait meant to make people see her as a loving mother, after the public had turned against her. Élisabeth Vigée Le Brun painted it in 1787, two years before the revolution, and the empty cradle on the left stands for a baby who had just died.
The Roman general Scipio Africanus returns a captured young bride to her fiancé instead of keeping her as a prize, a famous story about self-control. Nicolas-Guy Brenet painted it in 1788.

paintings.t: Virgil Reading the Aeneid to Augustus and Octavia
paintings.why: The poet Virgil reads from his epic poem the Aeneid to the emperor Augustus and his sister Octavia, who faints at the lines about her dead son Marcellus. Angelica Kauffmann painted this famous story in 1788.

paintings.t: Edward III with the Black Prince after the Battle of Crécy
paintings.why: King Edward III embraces his young son the Black Prince after the Battle of Crécy in 1346, proud of his first big victory. Benjamin West painted it in 1788 for King George III's series on Edward III.

paintings.t: Edward the Black Prince Receiving King John of France after Poitiers
paintings.why: After winning at Poitiers, the Black Prince treats the captured French king John with great courtesy. Benjamin West painted it in 1788 as an example of knightly manners.

Antoine Lavoisier, called the father of modern chemistry, sits in a detail from a double portrait by Jacques-Louis David in 1788. Lavoisier was guillotined during the Terror in 1794, even though his work was a gift to science.
Thomas Clarkson, who gathered evidence against the slave trade and traveled across Britain to campaign for abolition, sits writing in this portrait painted in 1788.

On July 14, 1789, Parisians stormed the Bastille, a royal fortress and prison, a day that became the symbol of the French Revolution. This painting by an unknown artist was made at the time and shows the crowd and cannon attacking the walls.

On July 14, 1790, the first anniversary of the Bastille, hundreds of thousands of people crowd the Champ de Mars in Paris to celebrate the new France in a festival of unity. This engraving shows the giant crowd.

paintings.t: The Arrival of Louis XVI in Paris
paintings.why: Louis XVI is brought back to Paris in a carriage in 1791 after he tried to flee the country, while the crowd watches in silence. His failed escape destroyed many people's trust in the king.

paintings.t: The Storming of the Tuileries, 10 August 1792
paintings.why: On August 10, 1792, the people of Paris attacked the Tuileries Palace, the king's home, and the monarchy fell. Jacques Bertaux painted the scene of fighting in 1793, soon after the event.

King Louis XVI was beheaded in front of a large crowd in Paris on January 21, 1793, when the revolutionaries turned from reform to ending the monarchy. This engraving of 1794 shows the whole square around the scaffold.

paintings.t: Coriolanus at the Gates of Rome
paintings.why: The Roman general Coriolanus, exiled by his own city, marches on Rome with an enemy army, but his mother and wife beg him to stop and he turns back. Franz Anton Maulbertsch painted this moving scene in the 1790s.

paintings.t: Louis XVI Pleading before the National Convention
paintings.why: Louis XVI is put on trial before the National Convention in December 1792, with the huge hall packed with deputies. This engraving by Reinier Vinkeles made the trial known across Europe.

paintings.t: The Defeat of the Spanish Armada
paintings.why: English fireships drift into the Spanish fleet at night in 1588 and the great Armada scatters in a blaze of flames. Philip James de Loutherbourg painted it in 1796, long after the event, to show off British sea power.

British boats land at the foot of the cliffs below Quebec in 1759, before the soldiers climbed up to the Plains of Abraham to fight the French. Hervey Smythe, a British officer who served with General Wolfe, made this view of the scene.

paintings.t: Portrait of Jean-Baptiste Belley, Deputy from Saint-Domingue
paintings.why: Jean-Baptiste Belley, a former slave who became a deputy to the French National Convention for Saint-Domingue (now Haiti), leans on a bust of an antislavery writer. Anne-Louis Girodet painted him in 1797, three years after France first abolished slavery.

A wooden fort sits on a hill above the North Saskatchewan River, with tents and people at its base. Paul Kane traveled across Canada in 1846–48, sketching the fur trade posts and the Indigenous peoples he met. Fort Edmonton was a major hub of the fur trade. It's an early picture of what is now a big city.

An Indigenous woman sits and weaves a blanket from wool on a simple loom. Paul Kane traveled to the Pacific coast and painted Indigenous crafts and daily life. His pictures help us see how people lived in the 1840s. It's a record of skill and tradition.
Thomas Jefferson, the writer of the Declaration of Independence and the third president of the United States, was painted by Rembrandt Peale in 1800, the year Jefferson was elected.
