paintings.why: A broken, twisted forest of shattered tree stumps stands in a landscape ripped by shell craters, under a bitter-sounding title. Paul Nash painted this in 1918 as an official war artist, and its irony made it one of the best-known pictures of World War I.
A.Y. Jackson, a founding member of Canada's Group of Seven, painted the green haze of a gas attack over the town of Liévin in 1918, while he was a Canadian war artist.

A bare, shell-torn hill called the Pimple glows red in the evening light near Vimy Ridge, where Canadian troops had fought in 1917. A.Y. Jackson, who later helped found the Group of Seven, painted it in 1918.
A single aeroplane sails among huge clouds in a dreamy, modern view of the war in the sky. C. R. W. Nevinson painted it in 1918 for Canada's war memorial collection.
Women work in a roaring factory filling shells for the war effort in 1918. Stanhope Forbes painted this scene of the many women who took on jobs once done by men while the soldiers were away.

Soldiers gather in a candlelit American Red Cross canteen at the front in France. Henry Ossawa Tanner, a Black American painter who lived in France, volunteered with the Red Cross and painted this in 1918.

paintings.t: Amiens, the Key of the West
paintings.why: The Australian war artist Arthur Streeton paints the soft green countryside around Amiens, the city that the Allies defended and then used for their big attack of August 1918.
Soft, glowing shapes in blue, green and orange seem to blend like notes. Kurt Schwitters painted this early abstraction in 1918, before he started making his famous Merz collages.

A huge crowd with flags and banners packs a Toronto street to celebrate the end of World War I. George Agnew Reid was a Canadian painter who was a leader in Toronto's art world. He painted this on the first Armistice Day in 1918 or 1919. It's a great record of public joy.

paintings.t: Forging 6-inch Shells - Cluff Ammunition Company, Toronto
paintings.why: Factory workers hammer glowing red-hot metal into shells in a busy, smoky factory. George Agnew Reid was commissioned to paint Canada's wartime work, including women and men in factories. The orange glow of the hot metal lights up the dark room. It's a record of the home front in World War I.

Paul Nash paints a wrecked, muddy landscape near Ypres in Belgium, with flooded craters and splintered trees. Made for the British government's war memorial project, it shows the destruction of the battlefield in 1919.

Wyndham Lewis shows an artillery position under fire in sharp, blocky shapes, like a machine of broken glass. He had served as a gunner himself before becoming an official war artist, and he painted this in 1919.

Smooth, brightly colored shapes like building blocks, boats and bottles sit together like a puzzle in a painting by Patrick Henry Bruce. An American who lived in Paris, Bruce painted this in 1919 and called it Peinture, French for painting.
A smoking factory in strong black and red shapes towers like a castle. Joseph Stella painted American factories and bridges as the new cathedrals of his adopted country, and made this one in 1919.

A side view of a face made from bits of paper, tickets, buttons and paint, in an early Merz collage by Kurt Schwitters in 1919. He used rubbish that he found on the street, called his art Merz, and made it into beauty.

The word UND, which means AND in German, is glued onto a collage of cut paper, scraps and paint. Kurt Schwitters made this Merz picture in 1919, using bits and pieces that he found, like tickets and labels.

paintings.t: Merzpicture 9 b (The Big Picture Of Me)
paintings.why: A mix of cut paper, bits of wood and splashes of color make a kind of self-portrait, with the title The Big Picture of Me. Kurt Schwitters, from Hanover in Germany, was an artist who could make a picture from almost anything.

paintings.t: Le Pont de glace à Québec
paintings.why: People cross the frozen St. Lawrence River at Quebec on an ice bridge in winter. Clarence Gagnon loved to paint Quebec's snow, villages and winter life. In cold winters the river froze solid, and people could walk across. It's a cheerful picture of Canadian winter.
l: Musée national des beaux-arts du Québec

paintings.why: A woman and a child stand in front of the Capitol on a poster for the League of Women Voters. The League was founded in 1920, the year the 19th Amendment gave American women the right to vote.

A huge worker holding a red flag strides over the crowded rooftops of a Russian city in this symbol of the Bolshevik revolution. Boris Kustodiev painted it in 1920, three years after the Bolsheviks took power.

paintings.t: Beat the Whites with the Red Wedge
paintings.why: A red triangle slices into a white circle in El Lissitzky's famous poster, a symbol of the Red Army defeating the White Army in the Russian Civil War. It was made in 1919 and 1920 and mixes politics with modern abstract art.
A Soviet poster of 1920 uses bold colors and cartoon figures in the style of the revolution's propaganda posters, which taught people about the new government in a country where many could not read.

A poster compares life before October 1917 and after it, using simple pictures so that everyone could understand the Bolshevik message. It was made by Stepan Mukharsky in 1920, during the Russian Civil War.

A tilted cube, a ball and a few bars float in a space that looks like a model of a future city. El Lissitzky invented the word Proun, a sort of 'project for the new', for his in-between works that were halfway between painting and architecture. This one is from 1920.

A circle with a spiral of rings seems to stretch like a spring toward a tiny black stick. El Lissitzky made his Prouns in the early 1920s as part of the explosion of new art after the Russian Revolution.

Overlapping balls and shapes in orange, gray and black make a kind of glowing machine. Ivan Kliun was one of the artists who worked with Malevich on Suprematism, and he painted this in the early 1920s.

Emily Carr is shown at her easel in a room with strong, simple shapes and bold colors. She was one of Canada's greatest painters, who lived much of her life in British Columbia with her pet monkey, dogs and her paintbrushes. She wasn't widely recognized until she was in her fifties, when the Group of Seven discovered her art. It's a picture of an artist at work.

Pilgrims and Wampanoag people gather for the harvest feast of 1621, which later became Thanksgiving. Jennie Augusta Brownscombe painted this version in 1925 after she had painted the subject many times.
Vladimir Lenin, the leader of the Bolshevik Revolution, lies in his coffin surrounded by red flags and officials in January 1924. Isaak Brodsky painted this memorial scene in 1925.

A stack of balconies, arches and tiny windows in bright blue, red and yellow makes an imaginary stage set. Alexandra Exter, a Russian artist who designed costumes and scenery for theaters in Paris and Moscow, painted this in 1925.
A railway line, a small shed and a tall dark building stand under an electric blue night sky in a painting by Oscar Bluemner from 1925. He loved to paint ordinary industrial places in deep color.

paintings.t: Merz 1925, 1. Relief in the Blue Square
paintings.why: Boards, pieces of metal and bright paint make a kind of relief sculpture on a wall. Kurt Schwitters, a German artist who built his own Merz buildings, made this around 1925.

Ghostly soldiers rise out of the fields near the Menin Gate, the great memorial at Ypres to the missing of World War I. Will Longstaff painted this in 1927 and it became one of Australia's most famous war paintings.

paintings.t: George Gershwin-I'll Build a Stairway to Paradise
paintings.why: Arthur Dove painted songs, and in this picture the jazzy tune by George Gershwin has turned into shapes and bright patches of color. He made it in 1927 as one of a group of pictures of music.

Tall carved totem poles stand against a dark forest and a sky in a First Nations village in northern British Columbia. Emily Carr visited Kitwancool (Gitanyow) in 1928 and painted the poles with great power and respect. She felt she was recording a culture that deserved to be remembered. It's one of her strongest paintings of the Northwest Coast.

A still, dark pool in the forest of Temagami in northern Ontario, with trees and rocks. David Milne painted the Canadian wilderness in thin, delicate watercolors. The mirror-like pool is quiet and mysterious. It's a peaceful picture of northern Ontario.

Florence Owens Thompson sits in a pea-pickers' camp in California in 1936, with her children turned away. Dorothea Lange's photograph for the government became the best-known image of the Great Depression.

paintings.t: Farmer and Sons Walking in the Face of a Dust Storm, Cimarron County, Oklahoma
paintings.why: A farmer and his sons walk bent against a huge dust cloud in Oklahoma in April 1936, during the Dust Bowl. Arthur Rothstein took this photograph for the government, which hired photographers to show how hard the Depression was.

paintings.t: Allie Mae Burroughs, Hale County, Alabama
paintings.why: Allie Mae Burroughs, the wife of a cotton sharecropper, looks straight at the camera in 1936. Walker Evans took this photograph for a project that became the book Let Us Now Praise Famous Men, about poor farming families during the Depression.

paintings.t: Frank Tengle, Bud Fields, and Floyd Burroughs, Cotton Sharecroppers
paintings.why: Three cotton sharecroppers sit together on a porch in Alabama in 1936. Walker Evans photographed families in Hale County for the government and a magazine, and the dignity in the faces made the photographs famous.

paintings.t: Floyd Burroughs, Cotton Sharecropper, Hale County, Alabama
paintings.why: Floyd Burroughs, a cotton sharecropper in Alabama, looks into the camera in 1936. Walker Evans photographed him and his family for a famous project about rural poverty in the Great Depression.

A man and woman carry their bags along an empty road in California in 1937, with a billboard above them that says 'Next time try the train.' Dorothea Lange's photo shows the ordeal of families who moved west to look for work.

A poster from the Works Progress Administration, the New Deal program that put millions of Americans back to work building roads, bridges and schools, as well as paying artists and writers. The workers and a wheat stalk show the idea that work lifts up the whole country.

paintings.t: Power Farming Displaces Tenants, Childress County, Texas
paintings.why: An empty farmhouse stands in a wide field of plowed furrows in Texas in 1938, a farm where tractors had taken the place of families who once worked the land as tenant farmers. Dorothea Lange photographed it for the government to show how the Depression and new machines pushed families off the land.

paintings.t: Ex-Slave with a Long Memory, Alabama
paintings.why: An elderly woman in Alabama who was born into slavery stands in front of her house in 1938. Dorothea Lange's photograph, taken during the Great Depression, honors a person who remembered a very different time in American history.

paintings.t: Jim Norris, Homesteader, Pie Town, New Mexico
paintings.why: Jim Norris, a homesteader in Pie Town, New Mexico, in 1940, photographed in rare color film by Russell Lee for the government. The color makes it feel as if the Depression is happening now.

paintings.t: School Children Singing, Pie Town, New Mexico
paintings.why: Children sing together in a school in Pie Town, New Mexico, in 1940, in a color photograph by Russell Lee. Pie Town was a farming community in the Depression years.

paintings.t: Gun Crew Loading a 5-inch 38 Caliber Gun
paintings.why: A sailor strains to load a big gun aboard a navy ship in 1940 in a powerful, poster-like painting. McClelland Barclay, an American illustrator who joined the US Navy as an artist, painted the sailors at work.

Ella Watson, a cleaning woman at a government office, stands with a mop and broom in front of an American flag in 1942. Gordon Parks, then a young photographer on his first assignment for the government, named it American Gothic as a tribute to Grant Wood's painting.

paintings.t: Ella Watson at Home, Washington, D.C.
paintings.why: Ella Watson with her family at home in Washington, D.C., in 1942, in a photograph by Gordon Parks. He followed her through her day to show the life of a working mother in the Depression years.
American soldiers crouch among tropical trees during an assault in the Pacific in 1943. Aaron Bohrod was an official US Army war artist who painted the war in the Pacific.

The great steel bridge at Nijmegen, which the Allies captured in September 1944 in the failed Operation Market Garden, arches across the river. Alex Colville, a Canadian war artist, painted it in 1944.
Army trucks roll along a road in the green hills of Yorkshire, England, where Canadian soldiers trained in 1944 before D-Day. Alex Colville was an official Canadian war artist.

paintings.t: Landing Craft Assault off Southern France
paintings.why: Landing craft head toward the coast in the Allied invasion of southern France in August 1944, in a painting by the Canadian war artist Alex Colville.
A Canadian tank rolls through the shattered streets of Ortona, Italy, where Canadian troops fought a fierce street battle in December 1943. Charles Comfort was an official Canadian war artist.
A line of Canadian tanks rolls over a green landscape in 1944. Bruno Bobak served as a Canadian war artist and made sketches and paintings of what he saw.
A dark London street during the wartime blackout, when all lights were turned off so that bombers could not find the city. Molly Bobak, a Canadian war artist, painted it in 1944.
An LVT, a tracked amphibious vehicle, drives up a beach on Saipan in June 1944 during the fighting in the Pacific. William F. Draper was a US Navy combat artist who went into battle with the troops.
Landing boats, soldiers and equipment fill Utah Beach in Normandy after the D-Day landings of June 6, 1944. Joseph Gary Sheahan, a combat artist, painted the scene in watercolor.

paintings.t: Loading of the Vultee Vengeance Planes
paintings.why: Ground crews load Vultee Vengeance dive-bombers in a busy scene from the war. Julien Binford painted it in 1944 as one of the US Army's combat artists.
Fire sweeps through a battlefield in the Pacific in 1944 in a painting by William F. Draper, a US Navy combat artist, who painted battles he had seen.

Trucks and landing craft sit on a muddy beach in the Netherlands in 1945, painted by the Canadian war artist Alex Colville. Canadian troops helped liberate the Netherlands in the last year of the war.

paintings.t: Night Air Attack before the Hitler Line
paintings.why: Flares and searchlights light up the sky over the Italian hills before an attack on the Hitler Line in 1944. Lawren P. Harris, an official Canadian war artist whose father was the famous Group of Seven painter Lawren Harris, painted it.

paintings.t: Canadian Women's Army Corps Brass Band
paintings.why: Women of the Canadian Women's Army Corps play in a brass band in 1945. Molly Bobak was a Canadian war artist who painted women's role in the armed forces.

paintings.t: Formal Japan Surrender aboard the U.S.S. Missouri
paintings.why: On September 2, 1945, aboard the battleship USS Missouri in Tokyo Bay, Japanese officials signed the surrender that ended World War II. Sidney Simon, a US Army artist, painted it.

A quiet field with open pits near the huts of Bergen-Belsen shows the horror of the Nazi concentration camp, which British and Canadian troops reached in April 1945. Alex Colville, a Canadian war artist, painted what he saw there, and the painting is a record of the Holocaust.

paintings.t: Alan Shepard in the Freedom 7 Capsule
paintings.why: Astronaut Alan Shepard sits in the tiny Freedom 7 capsule before his flight on May 5, 1961, when he became the first American in space. The flight lasted only 15 minutes.

Medics rush a wounded soldier to a waiting helicopter in a swirl of blue, in a painting of 1967 by Ronald A. Wilson, a US Army combat artist in Vietnam. Medical evacuation helicopters saved thousands of lives.
Ronald A. Wilson painted this night scene in purple shades in 1967, as a US Army combat artist. The name refers to the starlight scopes that helped soldiers see in the dark.
Flares light up the night sky while glowing lines of tracer fire cross the dark in this blue painting of 1967 by Ronald A. Wilson. It shows a night when a base answered a mortar attack.
A swirling, almost abstract picture of a trail through the jungle in Vietnam by James Pollock in 1967. He was one of the Army's combat artists, who were sent to record the war in their own style.

Our blue Earth rises over the gray edge of the Moon in this photograph taken by astronaut William Anders on Christmas Eve 1968 during Apollo 8, the first time people had seen the whole Earth from another world. It changed how many people thought about the planet.
Soldiers work on a big artillery gun in Vietnam in 1968 in a painting by David Fairrington. Fairrington was a member of the US Army combat art team, which sent artists to Vietnam to record the war.
A soldier carries a radio, the lifeline of a patrol, in a tall, bold painting by David Fairrington. He painted it in Vietnam in 1968 as part of the US Army's combat art program.
A soldier strides through golden grass in Vietnam in a painting of 1968 by David Fairrington. The Army's combat artists tried to show both the work and the feelings of the soldiers.
Vietnamese women in cone-shaped hats gather in a colorful, patterned scene by David Fairrington in 1968. The Army's combat artists also painted the Vietnamese people they met.
Two Vietnamese girls lean close to each other in a gentle painting by David Fairrington from 1968. It shows the everyday life of civilians alongside the war.
A Cobra attack helicopter, one of the most important aircraft of the Vietnam War, is painted in dark glassy shapes by Stephen H. Randall in 1968 as part of the US Army combat art program.
A helicopter waits on the ground in a muddy field in Vietnam, in a watercolor by Stephen H. Randall in 1968. Helicopters were everywhere in the Vietnam War, carrying troops and supplies.
Two soldiers lean over the edge of a bunker in Vietnam in a sketchy watercolor by Stephen H. Randall in 1968, made as part of the US Army's combat art program.
Medics treat a wounded soldier in a busy scene by Stephen H. Randall from 1968, one of the US Army combat artists sent to record the war in Vietnam.
Soldiers in dark, heavy shapes struggle in a tense scene by Stephen H. Randall from 1968. The US Army combat artists painted both the action and the feelings of the war.

paintings.t: A Man on the Moon (Buzz Aldrin, Apollo 11)
paintings.why: Buzz Aldrin stands on the Moon on July 20, 1969, in a photograph taken by Neil Armstrong, whose reflection you can see in Aldrin's gold visor. It is one of the most famous photographs ever taken.
A Saturn V rocket rises on a pillar of fire and smoke at the Kennedy Space Center on July 16, 1969, carrying the Apollo 11 crew to the Moon.

paintings.t: Buzz Aldrin's Bootprint on the Moon
paintings.why: A single bootprint in the gray Moon dust, taken by the Apollo 11 astronauts to study the lunar soil. This close-up has become a symbol of the first human steps on the Moon in July 1969.

paintings.t: Aldrin Looks Back at Tranquility Base
paintings.why: Buzz Aldrin looks back at the landing site, Tranquility Base, in the bright gray landscape of the Moon, with the lunar module Eagle behind him. Neil Armstrong took the photograph in July 1969.

paintings.t: Buzz Aldrin Descends the Lunar Module Ladder
paintings.why: Buzz Aldrin climbs down the ladder of the Apollo 11 lunar module Eagle onto the Moon in July 1969. Neil Armstrong took the picture, and Aldrin was the second person to walk on the Moon.

paintings.t: Buzz Aldrin and the U.S. Flag on the Moon
paintings.why: Buzz Aldrin stands beside the American flag on the Moon on July 20, 1969. The flag was held out by a wire so that it would look like it was flying in the airless Moon.

paintings.t: The Apollo 11 Crew: Armstrong, Collins and Aldrin
paintings.why: The crew of Apollo 11: Neil Armstrong, Michael Collins and Buzz Aldrin, in their white space suits. Armstrong and Aldrin walked on the Moon in July 1969 while Collins stayed in orbit.

paintings.t: Apollo 11 Rolls Out to the Launch Pad
paintings.why: The huge Saturn V rocket for Apollo 11 is carried slowly toward the launch pad on a giant crawler in May 1969. At 110 meters tall, it was the most powerful rocket ever built at the time.

paintings.t: Astronaut James Irwin Salutes the Flag, Apollo 15
paintings.why: Astronaut James Irwin salutes the flag beside the lunar module and the moon buggy, the lunar rover, in 1971. Apollo 15 was the first mission to use a rover on the Moon, and David Scott took the picture.
The whole Earth, round and blue and shining, photographed by the Apollo 17 astronauts on their way to the Moon in December 1972. The Blue Marble is one of the most reproduced images in history.
